items.title: Public market equivalent (PME)
items.text: The Kaplan-Schoar PME divides a fund's distributions, discounted at the S&P 500 total return, by its capital calls discounted the same way, all net of fees. Above 1.0 means the fund beat the index on a cash-flow-matched basis.
items.source_title: Private Equity Performance: Returns, Persistence and Capital Flows (NBER w9807 PDF)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER w9807 PDF: PME discounts cash flows at S&P 500 total return, net of fees; PME >1 outperformed.

items.title: DPI and TVPI
items.text: DPI (distributions to paid-in capital) counts only value returned to LPs in cash through exits or other liquidity events. TVPI (total value to paid-in) adds unrealized holdings at their current marks. A fund can show strong TVPI with near-zero DPI.
items.source_title: VC Fund Performance: Q1 2026
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Carta page defines DPI as realized via exit or liquidity event and TVPI as realized plus unrealized.

items.title: Private Equity Performance: Returns, Persistence and Capital Flows
items.text: Using Venture Economics fund data, found average PE returns net of fees roughly equal the S&P 500 with wide dispersion, strong persistence across a GP's successive funds, concave fund growth after good performance, and cyclical entry: funds raised in booms do worse. Introduced the PME measure.
items.source_title: Private Equity Performance: Returns, Persistence and Capital Flows (NBER w9807)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER page: Kaplan and Schoar, WP 9807 (2003), published JF vol 60, Aug 2005 as '...Capital Flows'; abstract matches.

items.title: Private Equity Performance: What Do We Know?
items.text: Using Burgiss cash-flow data on nearly 1,400 US funds, found average buyout funds beat the S&P 500 for most vintages, by 20% to 27% over fund life or over 3% a year. VC beat public equities in the 1990s but lagged in the 2000s.
items.source_title: Private Equity Performance: What Do We Know? (SSRN)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract matches (nearly 1,400 funds, Burgiss, 20% to 27%, >3% a year, VC 1990s vs 2000s); Crossref: JF 69(5) 2014.

items.title: Illiquid Alternative Asset Fund Modeling
items.text: A deterministic cash-flow model for illiquid funds: capital calls are a time-varying fraction of uncalled commitments, distributions a time-varying fraction of the fund's asset value, and returns are constant. Later work, such as Luxenberg et al. (2022), builds on it to model calls, distributions and asset value.
items.source_title: Strategic Asset Allocation with Illiquid Alternatives (arXiv 2207.07767), citing Takahashi and Alexander, JPM 28:90-100
items.checked: corrected by a second checker: arXiv paper confirms citation (JPM 2002) and model mechanics but says nothing about Yale or it being the standard tool.

items.title: The Economics of Private Equity Funds
items.text: Modeled expected manager revenue from fund contracts for 238 funds raised 1993 to 2006. About two thirds of expected revenue comes from fixed components such as management fees, not performance. Buyout managers scale fund size faster than VC managers, so buyout is the more scalable business.
items.source_title: The Economics of Private Equity Funds (SSRN)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN: Metrick and Yasuda, RFS 23(6) 2010; 238 funds 1993 to 2006; ~two-thirds fixed revenue; BO more scalable.

items.title: The Arithmetic of Active Management
items.text: Because passive investors hold the market and earn its return, active investors as a group must also earn the market return before costs. After their higher costs, the average actively managed dollar must therefore trail the average passively managed dollar. Contrary evidence reflects measurement errors.
items.source_title: The Arithmetic of Active Management (Financial Analysts Journal 47(1), 7-9)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Stanford reprint: Sharpe, FAJ 47(1) Jan/Feb 1991; arguments and 'improper measurement' match.

items.title: The Performance of Mutual Funds in the Period 1945-1964
items.text: Introduced Jensen's alpha, a CAPM-based measure of risk-adjusted performance. Across 115 funds from 1945 to 1964, funds on average could not beat a buy-and-hold strategy, even measured before management expenses, and few individual funds did better than chance would predict.
items.source_title: The Performance of Mutual Funds in the Period 1945-1964 (Journal of Finance 23(2), 389-416)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract: derives CAPM-based risk-adjusted measure, 115 funds 1945-1964, gross of expenses, chance; Crossref JF 23(2) 1968 (SSRN lists 1967).

items.title: On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance
items.text: Using survivor-bias-free data, common factors in stock returns, including one-year momentum, plus fund expenses almost fully explain persistence in mutual fund returns. The only strong unexplained persistence is the underperformance of the worst funds, and the results do not support the existence of skilled or informed managers.
items.source_title: On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance (Journal of Finance 52(1), 57-82)
items.checked: corrected by a second checker: doi.org/Wiley page blocked; Crossref confirms Carhart, JF 52(1) 1997 and abstract; 'four-factor model became the standard benchmark' is not in the source.

items.title: Mutual Fund Flows and Performance in Rational Markets
items.text: A rational model in which skilled managers face decreasing returns to scale. Investors chase past performance, flows grow funds until expected excess returns vanish, so performance does not persist and average funds do not beat passive benchmarks, even though managers have real and varied skill.
items.source_title: Mutual Fund Flows and Performance in Rational Markets (Journal of Political Economy 112(6), 1269-1295)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: UChicago page and Crossref: Berk and Green, JPE 112(6) 2004; abstract consistent.

items.title: Luck versus Skill in the Cross-Section of Mutual Fund Returns
items.text: The aggregate portfolio of US equity mutual funds is close to the market portfolio, so high active costs show up as lower investor returns. Bootstrap simulations show few funds earn enough to cover costs; before expenses, the tails show some genuine skill, both good and bad.
items.source_title: Luck versus Skill in the Cross-Section of Mutual Fund Returns (Journal of Finance 65(5), 1915-1947)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract matches; Crossref: JF 65(5) 2010.

items.title: Relative Strength Index (RSI)
items.text: Wilder's RSI is a 0 to 100 momentum oscillator: RSI = 100 - 100/(1 + RS), where RS is average gain over average loss, by default over 14 periods with Wilder smoothing. Wilder treated readings above 70 as overbought and below 30 as oversold.
items.source_title: Relative Strength Index (RSI)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: ChartSchool: RS = avg gain / avg loss, 14 periods, Wilder smoothing, 70/30, 1978 book.

items.title: Average True Range (ATR)
items.text: True range is the largest of: today's high minus low, high minus prior close, or low minus prior close (absolute values). ATR, from Wilder (1978), averages true range over 14 periods, then smooths it as (prior ATR x 13 + current TR) / 14. It measures volatility, not direction, and is used for stop and position sizing.
items.source_title: Average True Range (ATR) and Average True Range Percent (ATRP)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: ChartSchool: three true range methods, Wilder 1978, 14 periods, (prior ATR x 13 + TR)/14, volatility not direction.

items.title: Average Directional Index (ADX)
items.text: Wilder's directional movement system uses +DI and -DI (smoothed directional movement divided by smoothed true range) for direction, and ADX, a smoothed average of their normalized difference, for trend strength. Default is 14 periods. Wilder saw ADX above 25 as a strong trend and below 20 as no trend.
items.source_title: Average Directional Index (ADX)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: ChartSchool: +DI/-DI from smoothed DM over smoothed ATR, ADX from smoothed DX, 14 periods, above 25 strong and below 20 no trend.

items.title: Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD)
items.text: MACD, invented by Gerald Appel in the late 1970s, is the 12-day EMA minus the 26-day EMA of closing prices. The signal line is a 9-day EMA of MACD, and the histogram is MACD minus signal. It turns two trend-following averages into a momentum oscillator.
items.source_title: MACD (Moving Average Convergence/Divergence Oscillator)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: ChartSchool: Appel, late seventies, 12-26 EMA, 9-day signal, histogram = MACD minus signal.

items.title: Bollinger Bands
items.text: John Bollinger's bands are a moving average (default 20 periods) with upper and lower bands a multiple (default 2) of the population standard deviation away. They show whether price is high or low relative to recent volatility. Companion measures are %b (position within the bands) and BandWidth (band width relative to the middle band).
items.source_title: Bollinger Bands
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: bollingerbands.com: 20 periods, 2 standard deviations, population SD, %b and BandWidth described.

items.title: Faber timing model (10-month moving average)
items.text: Faber's timing model holds an asset class when its month-end price is above its 10-month simple moving average and moves to cash otherwise, checked only on the last day of each month. Faber says the 10-month average corresponds most closely to the 200-day moving average.
items.source_title: Timing Model
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page confirms 10-month SMA, buy signals versus moving to cash, month-end-only updates, and 'corresponds closest to the 200 day moving average'. It does not spell out the rule in one sentence; the SSRN paper does. Page says the model was first published in 2006 (journal version 2007).

items.title: Cyclically adjusted P/E (CAPE, Shiller PE, PE10)
items.text: CAPE divides the index price by the average of the previous 10 years of inflation-adjusted earnings, smoothing the business cycle out of the denominator. It is also called the Shiller PE or PE 10. Multpl credits its data to Robert Shiller.
items.source_title: Shiller PE Ratio
items.checked: corrected by a second checker: 10-year inflation-adjusted earnings definition confirmed. The page does not mention Campbell and Shiller's findings or shillerdata.com, removed. The 1998 as_of date is not on this page.

items.title: The Fed model
items.text: The Fed model compares the stock market's earnings yield (inverse of P/E) with the nominal 10-year Treasury yield, calling stocks cheap when the earnings yield is higher. It came from an unnamed Fed report and has no official endorsement. Asness (2003) found it has no power to forecast long-term real stock returns.
items.source_title: Fight the Fed Model
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: AQR: earnings yield vs nominal rates, 'allegedly found in the annals of a Fed report', not officially endorsed, no power to forecast long-term real returns, 2003.

items.title: New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems
items.text: Wilder's 1978 book introduced the RSI, Average True Range and the directional movement system (ADX, +DI, -DI). Its 14-period defaults and smoothing method remain the standard settings in charting software.

items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Library record: Wilder, New concepts in technical trading systems, Trend Research, Greensboro N.C., 1978, 141 pp.

items.title: Technical Analysis: Power Tools for Active Investors
items.text: Appel's 2005 book presents trading models built on MACD, which he describes as an indicator he invented in the late 1970s. It is the creator's own account of how to construct and use MACD.

items.title: Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns
items.text: Testing moving-average and trading-range-break rules on the Dow Jones index from 1897 to 1986 with bootstrap methods, the authors found returns after buy signals exceeded returns after sell signals, which were negative. The patterns were inconsistent with random walk, AR(1), GARCH-M and EGARCH models.
items.source_title: Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns (IDEAS/RePEc record)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: RePEc: JF 47(5) 1731-1764, 1992. Abstract matches (DJIA 1897-1986, buy beats sell, sell returns negative, four null models).

items.title: Data-Snooping, Technical Trading Rule Performance, and the Bootstrap
items.text: Using White's Reality Check over a universe of 7,846 rules and 100 years of Dow data, the authors found the best rule beat the benchmark in 1897-1986 even after adjusting for data snooping. In 1987-1996, out of sample, there was scant evidence of value: the best rule was not statistically significant.
items.source_title: Data-Snooping, Technical Trading Rule Performance, and the Bootstrap (LSE FMG Discussion Paper 303)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: FMG DP303 (Oct 1998): 7,846 rules in body, 100 years of DJIA, scant evidence for 1987-1996. Crossref confirms JF 54(5) 1647-1691, 1999.

items.title: A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation
items.text: Faber proposed a simple month-end trend rule (hold an asset above its 10-month moving average, else cash) across asset classes. The 2013 update on SSRN, adding 2008-2012 data, reports the models performed well in real time, with equity-like returns and bond-like volatility and drawdowns.
items.source_title: A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation (SSRN, 2013 update)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN: Faber, Journal of Wealth Management Spring 2007; 2013 update adds 2008-2012 data, 'equity like returns with bond like volatility and drawdowns'.

items.title: Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency
items.text: Strategies that buy past winners and sell past losers earned significant positive returns over 3 to 12 month holding periods, not explained by systematic risk or delayed reactions to common factors. Part of the first-year excess return reverses over the next two years. This is the founding cross-sectional momentum paper.
items.source_title: Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers (IDEAS/RePEc record)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: RePEc: JF 48(1) 65-91, 1993. Abstract matches (3-12 month holding periods, partial reversal over next two years).

items.title: Time Series Momentum
items.text: Across 58 liquid equity index, currency, commodity and bond futures, an asset's own recent returns predict its future returns. Returns persist for 1 to 12 months then partly reverse. A diversified strategy earns large abnormal returns, has little exposure to standard factors, and does best in extreme markets.
items.source_title: Time Series Momentum (SSRN)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract: 58 instruments, persistence 1 to 12 months then partial reversal, 'performs best during extreme markets'. Crossref confirms JFE 104(2) 228-250, 2012.

items.title: A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing
items.text: Building a time-series momentum strategy across markets with data back to 1880, the authors find trend following was consistently profitable over roughly 110 years, across many economic conditions. They also examine how growth in strategy assets and higher cross-market correlations since the credit crisis affect results.
items.source_title: A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: AQR: JPM, Oct 31, 2017. Back to 1880, profitable 'over the next 110 years', covers rising assets and higher correlations since the credit crisis.

items.title: Foundations of Technical Analysis: Computational Algorithms, Statistical Inference, and Empirical Implementation
items.text: The authors automate chart-pattern recognition (such as head-and-shoulders and double bottoms) with nonparametric kernel regression and apply it to US stocks from 1962 to 1996. Several patterns shift the distribution of subsequent daily returns, suggesting technical patterns carry some incremental information.
items.source_title: Foundations of Technical Analysis (NBER Working Paper 7613)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER w7613 (Mar 2000), JF 55(4) 2000. Kernel regression, US stocks 1962-1996, incremental information.

items.title: What Do We Know About the Profitability of Technical Analysis?
items.text: Surveying the literature, the authors count 95 modern studies: 56 positive for technical trading profits, 20 negative and 19 mixed. Gains were stronger in currency and futures markets than in stocks. They warn that data snooping, ex post rule selection and risk and cost estimation weaken most results.
items.source_title: What Do We Know About The Profitability Of Technical Analysis? (IDEAS/RePEc record)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: RePEc: JES 21(4) 786-826, 2007. 95 modern studies: 56 positive, 20 negative, 19 mixed. Caveats match.

items.title: Stock Prices, Earnings and Expected Dividends
items.text: Using US data from 1871 to 1986, the authors find a long historical average of real earnings is a good predictor of the present value of future real dividends. Prices are too volatile for simple present value models, which implies long-horizon returns are forecastable. This is the root of the CAPE idea.
items.source_title: Stock Prices, Earnings and Expected Dividends (NBER Working Paper 2511)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER w2511, JF 43(3) 661-676 (July 1988). Abstract: US data 1871-1986, excess volatility implies forecastable long-horizon returns.

items.title: Valuation Ratios and the Long-Run Stock Market Outlook
items.text: Using US data from 1871 and 12 countries since 1970, the authors find P/E and dividend-price ratios do poorly at forecasting dividend, earnings or productivity growth and are mainly useful for forecasting future price changes, against simple efficient-markets models. Published in the Journal of Portfolio Management (1998), updated 2001 as NBER w8221.
items.source_title: Valuation Ratios and the Long-Run Stock Market Outlook: An Update (NBER Working Paper 8221)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER w8221 (Apr 2001) updates the 1998 JPM 24(2) paper. US data 1871-2000 plus 12 countries since 1970. Abstract matches.

items.title: Predicting Excess Stock Returns Out of Sample: Can Anything Beat the Historical Average?
items.text: Answering Goyal and Welch, the authors show that predictors with in-sample power, such as valuation ratios, beat the historical average out of sample once sensible restrictions are placed on coefficient signs and return forecasts. The gain is small but economically meaningful, and a true predictor can still underperform for long stretches.
items.source_title: Predicting the Equity Premium Out of Sample (NBER Working Paper 11468)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER w11468, RFS 21 (July 2008) 1509-1531. Abstract matches.

items.title: A Comprehensive Look at the Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction
items.text: Testing dividend and earnings yields, interest rates and other popular predictors, the authors find many look useful in sample, but none would have beaten the historical average equity premium out of sample for a real-time investor, and most would have hurt. They conclude the equity premium has not been predictable in practice.

items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER w10483 (May 2004), RFS 21(4) 1455-1508, 2008. Abstract matches. NBER page misspells the name as 'Goval'.

items.title: Dividend Yields and Expected Stock Returns
items.text: The forecasting power of dividend yields rises with the horizon: regressions on D/P explain under 5% of monthly or quarterly return variance but often more than 25% of two- to four-year return variance. The authors attribute this to slowly moving, time-varying expected returns that create temporary price components.

items.title: Fight the Fed Model
items.text: Asness argues the Fed model, which compares the earnings yield with nominal Treasury yields, is intuitive but empirically wrong: it has no power to forecast long-term real stock returns, while the plain P/E has worked well. items.title: Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions
items.text: Treats liquidating a large position as a trade-off between market impact cost (trading fast) and price risk (trading slow). Derives an efficient frontier of execution schedules under linear temporary and permanent impact, shows an even-slice schedule is never optimal for a risk-averse trader, and defines liquidity-adjusted VaR.
items.source_title: Journal of Risk 3(2): 5-39
items.checked: corrected by a second checker: Crossref confirms Almgren and Chriss, Journal of Risk 3(2) 5-39, 2001; 'draft dated December 2000' not verifiable (author PDF unreachable), removed; abstract not served, content matches known paper.

items.title: Anomalous Price Impact and the Critical Nature of Liquidity in Financial Markets
items.text: Proposes a theory in which the average supply and demand profile is V-shaped and nearly vanishes at the current price. This forces large orders to be split, explaining long memory in order signs, and makes price impact grow roughly with the square root of order size rather than linearly: the square-root impact law.
items.source_title: Physical Review X 1, 021006 (arXiv:1105.1694)
items.authors: Toth, Lemperiere, Deremble, de Lataillade, Kockelkoren, Bouchaud
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: arXiv: six authors, May 2011, Physical Review X 1, 021006 (2011); abstract: V-shaped profile vanishing at price, metaorder splitting, long memory, square-root impact.

items.title: Price Impact
items.text: A review of how price impact is measured and modeled. Signed order flow and price changes are strongly linked, but the impact of trades is neither linear in volume nor permanent. Impact is how private information enters prices, and random order-flow fluctuations also add to volatility.
items.source_title: Price Impact (arXiv:0903.2428), review chapter
items.checked: corrected by a second checker: arXiv page (March 13 2009) shows no Encyclopedia of Quantitative Finance reference; abstract content confirmed.

items.title: On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets
items.text: If gathering information is costly, prices cannot fully reflect it, or no one would be paid to gather it. Equilibrium needs an 'equilibrium degree of disequilibrium' where prices are partly informative and informed traders earn a return on research. Noise is needed for trade; perfectly efficient markets would be thin.
items.source_title: American Economic Review 70(3): 393-408
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: AEA PDF: AER 70(3) 393-408, June 1980; 'equilibrium degree of disequilibrium' present; noise needed; informative markets very thin.

items.title: Noise
items.text: Argues that noise, in the sense of a large number of small events, makes trading in financial markets possible and lets us observe prices. It also makes markets somewhat inefficient while often stopping anyone from exploiting the inefficiency, and makes theories about markets very hard to test.
items.source_title: The Journal of Finance 41(3): 528-543
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: Black, JF 41(3) 528-543, July 1986; abstract: noise makes trading possible, somewhat inefficient, hard to test theories.

items.title: Noise Trader Risk in Financial Markets
items.text: Models irrational noise traders whose unpredictable beliefs move prices. Because those beliefs are unpredictable, rational arbitrageurs face risk and cannot bet aggressively against them, so prices can stay far from fundamentals and noise traders can even earn higher expected returns. Helps explain excess volatility and closed-end fund discounts.
items.source_title: Journal of Political Economy 98: 703-738
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: RePEc: JPE 98(4) 703-738, 1990, four authors; abstract: unpredictable noise traders move prices, arbitrageurs limited, noise traders can earn higher returns, explains anomalies (Crossref fetch failed).

items.title: The Limits of Arbitrage
items.text: Real-world arbitrage takes capital and carries risk, and is done by a small number of specialists using other people's money. As a result arbitrage can fail in extreme situations, when prices move far from fundamentals, and the model predicts where anomalies are likely to persist.
items.source_title: The Journal of Finance 52(1): 35-55
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Crossref: JF 52(1) 35-55, March 1997; abstract: capital and risk, few specialists using others' money, ineffective in extremes, where anomalies persist.

items.title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk
items.text: Shows that people's choices under risk violate expected utility. People value gains and losses relative to a reference point, with a value function concave for gains, convex for losses and steeper for losses (loss aversion). They underweight probable outcomes versus certain ones and overweight small probabilities.
items.source_title: Econometrica 47(2): 263-292
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Econometric Society page: Econometrica 47(2) 263-292, 1979; abstract: critique of EU, certainty effect, value function concave gains, convex losses, steeper for losses, low probabilities overweighted.

items.title: Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth: The Common Stock Investment Performance of Individual Investors
items.text: Using 66,465 households at a large discount broker in 1991 to 1996, finds the most active traders earned 11.4% a year against 17.9% for the market, while the average household earned 16.4%. Overconfidence explains the heavy trading and poor results.

items.title: Taleb (2019), How much data do you need? A pre-asymptotic metric for fat-tailedness
items.text: Proposes kappa, a measure scaled from 0 (Gaussian, thinnest) to 1 (maximally fat-tailed), based on how fast the law of large numbers works for sums of n terms. Meant to tell how many observations are needed and to compare distribution classes where kurtosis or tail index fail. International Journal of Forecasting 35(2), 677-686, April 2019.
items.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? An Operational, Pre-Asymptotic Metric for Fat-tailedness (arXiv 1802.05495; DOI 10.1016/j.ijforecast.2018.10.003)
items.publisher: International Journal of Forecasting (Elsevier); preprint on arXiv
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: arXiv abstract matches; Crossref: IJF 35(2) 677-686, April 2019, sole author Taleb.

items.title: Taleb's kappa: formula
items.text: With S_n the sum of n i.i.d. draws and M(n) = E|S_n - E(S_n)| (mean absolute deviation of the sum), kappa(n0, n) = 2 - [log(n) - log(n0)] / log[M(n)/M(n0)]. Equivalently M(n)/M(n0) = (n/n0)^(1/(2-kappa)). Shorthand kappa_n0 uses n = n0 + 1; kappa_1 compares one draw with two.
items.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3, Definition 1 and Eq. 1)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Eq. 1 and M(n)/M(n0)=(n/n0)^(1/(2-kappa)) match; kappa_n0 = kappa(n0, n0+1).

items.title: Kappa for the Gaussian is 0
items.text: The paper states kappa equals 0 for the Gaussian: the mean absolute deviation of a sum grows with the square root of n, the fastest convergence. For stable laws with tail exponent alpha at least 1, kappa = 2 - alpha.
items.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Paper: kappa=0 for Gaussian; kappa=2-alpha for stable with alpha>=1.

items.title: Kappa for the Cauchy is 1
items.text: From the paper's stable-law relation kappa = 2 - alpha, the Cauchy (stable alpha = 1) has kappa = 1, the maximum: averaging more Cauchy draws does not shrink dispersion at all, so no sample is large enough. The paper also notes a high-sigma lognormal behaves like a one-tailed Cauchy, kappa near 1.
items.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Cauchy value is derived from kappa=2-alpha as the item says (paper gives no explicit Cauchy row); lognormal high-sigma 'one-tailed Cauchy', kappa near 1 confirmed.

items.title: Kappa for Student T with alpha 3 (a common fit for equity returns)
items.text: Table II gives Student T alpha = 3: kappa_1 = 0.29, kappa_1,30 = 0.191, kappa_1,100 = 0.159. Pareto alpha = 3 is fatter: 0.465, 0.3246, 0.281. The exponential has kappa_1 of about 0.21. Values between 0 and 1 rank how much extra data a distribution needs relative to a Gaussian.
items.source_title: How Much Data Do You Need? (arXiv 1802.05495v3, Tables I and II)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Table II: Student alpha=3 0.29/0.191/0.159; Pareto 0.465/0.3246/0.281; exponential kappa_1 ~ .21 in Table I.

items.title: Taleb and Douady (2013), Mathematical definition, mapping, and detection of (anti)fragility
items.text: Defines fragility and antifragility as negative or positive sensitivity to a semi-measure of dispersion and volatility (a 'vega'), model-free and applicable to any payoff with a distribution. Proposes a simple detection heuristic said to reveal hidden risks from size, forecasting and bank tail exposures. Quantitative Finance 13(11), 1677-1689, November 2013.
items.source_title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility (arXiv 1208.1189; DOI 10.1080/14697688.2013.800219)
items.publisher: Quantitative Finance (Taylor and Francis); preprint on arXiv
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: arXiv abstract matches (vega, model-free heuristic, size/forecasting/bank hidden risks); Crossref: Quant Finance 13(11) 1677-1689, Nov 2013.

items.title: Fragility in one sentence (Taleb-Douady)
items.text: Fragility is the sensitivity of the left-tail shortfall below a threshold K (the integral of (x - Omega) f(x) from minus infinity to K, not conditioned on probability) to a change in the left semi-deviation of the distribution; an engine can estimate it by bumping volatility and measuring how much expected tail loss grows.
items.source_title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility (arXiv 1208.1189v1)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF defines fragility as sensitivity of unconditional left-tail shortfall xi(K,s-) = integral (x-Omega) f(x) to left semi-deviation.

items.title: Taleb-Douady detection heuristic
items.text: Their heuristic measures how a valuation or payoff responds to finite shifts of each parameter up and down by a step delta, and compares the two changes as a second-order (convexity) test: losses that accelerate with larger shocks signal fragility. The paper claims this beats stress testing and Value-at-Risk at revealing hidden tail exposure.
items.source_title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility (arXiv 1208.1189)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF heuristic: finite shifts Delta p, second-order ratio H vs 1; abstract says it outperforms stress testing and VaR.

Third revised edition posted on arXiv September 17, 2025 (v4).

items.title: Taleb on ruin and ergodicity
items.text: Taleb separates ensemble probability (outcomes across many people at once) from time probability (one person repeating a bet). With any chance of ruin these diverge: a repeated bet with ruin risk reaches eventual bust with 100% probability, so average-of-population returns do not apply to the individual and cost-benefit analysis breaks down. Survival comes first.

items.title: Damodaran's narrative-to-numbers method
items.text: Damodaran's method ties every valuation input to a story and every story to an input. For a young or growth firm the story drives revenue growth, a target operating margin, and reinvestment set by a sales-to-capital ratio; risk enters the discount rate and survival risk enters as a separate probability of failure.

items.text: Studies 97 published cross-sectional return predictors. Journal of Finance 71(1), pages 5 to 32, February 2016. Concludes that investors learn about mispricing from academic publications, so published anomalies shrink after they become known.

items.title: Anomaly returns are 26% lower out-of-sample
items.text: Across 97 published predictors, long-short portfolio returns are 26% lower in the out-of-sample period (after the original sample ends, before publication). The authors treat this as an upper bound on the data-mining effect.

items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract: 97 variables, 26% lower out-of-sample; 'out-of-sample decline is an upper bound estimate of data mining effects.'

items.title: Anomaly returns are 58% lower after publication
items.text: Predictor portfolio returns are 58% lower after academic publication. The gap over the 26% out-of-sample decline implies about a 32% further drop attributable to publication-informed trading. Declines are larger for predictors with higher in-sample returns.

items.title: Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016): ...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
items.text: Argues that with hundreds of tested factors, the usual t-ratio of 2.0 is far too lenient and that "most claimed research findings in financial economics are likely false." Review of Financial Studies 29(1), pages 5 to 68, 2016 (NBER w20592, 2014).
items.source_title: ...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns (NBER Working Paper 20592)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: NBER page: quote verbatim in abstract, t-ratio 2.0 cited; RFS 29(1) 5-68, 2016; w20592 issued Oct 2014.

items.title: 316 factors catalogued in the literature
items.text: Harvey, Liu and Zhu write "We catalogue 316 different factors" proposed to explain the cross-section of returns. Testing that many candidates on the same data makes some false positives nearly certain unless significance thresholds rise.
items.source_title: ...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns (NBER w20592 full text)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF contains 'We catalogue 316 different factors.' Dated October 2014.

items.title: New factors should clear a t-ratio above 3.0
items.text: Accounting for multiple testing, the authors estimate a newly discovered factor needs a t-ratio greater than 3.0, versus the conventional 2.0. An engine can treat a backtest t-statistic between 2 and 3 as weak evidence.
items.source_title: ...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns (NBER Working Paper 20592)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Abstract: new factor needs 'a t-ratio greater than 3.0' versus usual 2.0. Last sentence is editorial.

items.title: Harvey and Liu (2015): Backtesting and the haircut Sharpe ratio
items.text: Provides a multiple-testing framework to compute the appropriate haircut for any reported backtest Sharpe ratio, given how many strategies were tried, plus a profit hurdle a strategy must clear to count as significant. Journal of Portfolio Management, Fall 2015.
items.source_title: Backtesting (SSRN abstract)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: SSRN abstract supports haircut framework and profit hurdle. SSRN page lists no journal; JPM Fall 2015 confirmed on the Duke author copy.

items.title: The flat 50% Sharpe haircut is a rule of thumb, and a mistake
items.text: Practitioners commonly discount backtest Sharpe ratios by 50%. Harvey and Liu write "it is a serious mistake to use the usual 50% haircut" because the right haircut depends on the number of tests and the Sharpe level.
items.source_title: Backtesting (Journal of Portfolio Management, Fall 2015)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Duke PDF: 'We argue that it is a serious mistake to use the usual 50% haircut.' JPM Fall 2015.

items.title: Haircuts are nonlinear: at most 25% when Sharpe exceeds 1.0
items.text: The multiple-testing haircut is nonlinear: the highest Sharpe ratios are only moderately penalized while marginal ones are heavily penalized. In their examples the haircut is at most 25% when the Sharpe ratio exceeds 1.0, but nearly 50% for a weak E/P strategy with 50 trials.
items.unit: percent maximum haircut for Sharpe above 1.0
items.source_title: Backtesting (Journal of Portfolio Management, Fall 2015)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF: haircut nonlinear; 'when the Sharpe ratio is greater than 1.0, the haircut is at most 25%'; 'almost 50%' for least profitable E/P strategy at 50 trials.

items.title: Sharpe 0.75 cut to 0.32 after 200 tests (about 60% haircut)
items.text: Worked example: an annual Sharpe ratio of 0.75 has a single-test p-value of 0.0008, but with 200 tests the adjusted p-value is 0.15, implying an adjusted Sharpe of 0.32, a reduction of roughly 60%.
items.source_title: Backtesting (Journal of Portfolio Management, Fall 2015)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: PDF: SR 0.75, p 0.0008, N=200 gives pM=0.15, adjusted SR 0.32, reduction approximately 60%.

items.title: The ten pitfalls and their fixes, one line each

items.title: SR 11-7 definition of model risk
items.text: The Federal Reserve and OCC define model risk as "the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports." items.title: SR 11-7 definition of a model
items.text: A model is "a quantitative method, system, or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories, techniques, and assumptions to process input data into quantitative estimates." Under this definition a backtested trading signal counts as a model.
items.source_title: SR 11-7: Guidance on Model Risk Management (Federal Reserve and OCC, April 4, 2011)

items.title: Effective challenge
items.text: SR 11-7's guiding principle: "critical analysis by objective, informed parties that can identify model limitations and produce appropriate changes." It adds that "Effective challenge depends on a combination of incentives, competence, and influence." This is the role the portfolio manager's complaint asks the engine to play.

items.title: SR 11-7's three validation elements, with backtesting as outcomes analysis

items.text: Machine Learning 45(1), 5-32. "The generalization error for forests converges a.s. to a limit as the number of trees in the forest becomes large" and depends on tree strength and correlation between trees. Random feature selection gives error rates comparable to AdaBoost, more robust to noise, with out-of-bag estimates of error and variable importance.

items.title: Angelopoulos and Bates (2021): a gentle introduction to conformal prediction
items.text: arXiv 2107.07511 (v6, December 2022). Practical guide to distribution-free uncertainty sets that are "guaranteed to contain the ground truth with a user-specified probability, such as 90%," wrapped around any fitted model, with sections on covariate shift, distribution drift and a time-series example.
items.source_title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: v6 dated 2022-12-07; quote verbatim; sections 4.5 covariate shift, 4.6 distribution drift, 5.3 time series.

items.title: Split conformal coverage guarantee
items.text: With n calibration points exchangeable with the test point, split conformal sets satisfy 1 - alpha <= P(Y_test in C(X_test)) <= 1 - alpha + 1/(n+1). The threshold is the empirical quantile of calibration scores at level ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n. The guarantee is marginal (on average over points), not conditional on today's regime.
items.source_title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification (PDF)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Eq. (1) bounds 1-alpha to 1-alpha+1/(n+1), quantile ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n, marginal guarantee all in PDF.

items.title: Conformal guarantees assume exchangeability, which return series violate
items.text: Angelopoulos and Bates' Theorem 1 assumes calibration and test points are i.i.d.; their time-series example notes "these data points are not exchangeable or i.i.d.; adjacent data points will be correlated." Under drift, coverage can fall below 1 - alpha by an amount tied to distribution shift, so empirical coverage must be monitored in walk-forward tests.
items.source_title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification (PDF)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Theorem 1 assumes i.i.d.; quote verbatim; Theorem 4 bounds coverage loss by TV distance.

Embeds each EMS exchange rate in 6 lags, picks the closest historical patterns (about 2% of the sample), fits a local least-squares regression on what followed, and adds a simultaneous version that also uses related currencies.

Practitioner text covering financial data bars, labeling (triple-barrier, meta-labeling), sample weights for overlapping outcomes, purged k-fold cross-validation, feature importance under substitution effects, bet sizing and combinatorial purged backtesting.

items.title: Triple-barrier labeling
items.text: A label is set by whichever barrier the price path hits first: an upper profit-taking barrier (label 1), a lower stop-loss barrier (label -1), or a vertical time barrier ending the trade. Horizontal barriers scale with recent volatility, typically a multiple of the daily standard deviation of log returns. From Lopez de Prado (2018), section 3.4.
items.source_title: Does Meta Labeling Add to Signal Efficacy? (Hudson & Thames)
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Hudson & Thames (Singh, Joubert, 30 Apr 2019) supports labels and volatility scaling; book section 3.4 'The Triple-Barrier Method' confirmed via O'Reilly TOC.

items.title: Meta-labeling
items.text: A primary model picks the side (long or short); a secondary model learns "whether we should act or pass on the opportunity" and how large to bet. It aims to raise precision by "filtering out the false positives." Introduced in Lopez de Prado (2018), chapter 3.
items.source_title: Meta Labeling (A Toy Example) (Hudson & Thames)
items.checked: corrected by a second checker: Quotes and chapter 3 attribution confirmed; Joubert JFDS 4(3) 2022 citation not on page, removed.

items.title: Substitution effects in feature importance
items.text: "A substitution effect takes place when two or more explanatory variables share a substantial amount of information." Then feature importance methods "may not be able to determine robustly which variables are significant." Lopez de Prado presents Clustered Feature Importance, "robust to linear as well as non-linear substitution effects." Engine note: permutation importance can understate each of two correlated features.

items.speaker: Matt Bornstein, Guido Appenzeller, Martin Casado (a16z)

items.title: a16z: data is not a magic moat

items.speaker: Martin Casado and Peter Lauten (a16z)

items.title: Pearl: proof of work by matrix multiplication
items.text: Pearl is a Bitcoin-style Layer 1 that "replaces SHA-256 hashing with matrix multiplication as its proof of work function." "The chain has a fixed 2.1B PRL supply and targets 194-second blocks." Miners commit to their input matrices first, and the result is verifiable by other nodes without re-running the full workload.

items.title: Pearl's duplex work: the same matmuls earn twice
items.text: "That work is matrix multiplications, the core math behind AI inference (running a trained model to answer requests)." Bankless describes Pearl as a fork of Bitcoin that launched in April, with launch inference prices up to roughly 75% below a major provider's standard rates, potentially subsidized by mining rewards.

items.title: SpaceX 180-day lockup on employee and pre-IPO shares ends Dec 8, 2026 (Form 424B4)
items.text: Per SpaceX's Form 424B4 (filed Jun 12, 2026) as summarized by BFA Wealth (facts checked Oct 20, 2026), employee and other pre-IPO shares are under a 180-day lockup ending Dec 8, 2026, with staged employee releases before then: up to 20% on Aug 6 (second full trading day after Q2 earnings), 7% each at 70, 90, 105, 120 and 135 days (Aug 20, Sep 9, Sep 24, Oct 9, Oct 26), 28% on the second full trading day after Q3 earnings (reported Oct 20, so Oct 22), and the remainder on Dec 8. Musk's shares are locked 366 days to Jun 12, 2027; certain other holders release in stages from the Q4 2026 through the Q2 2027 earnings reports. items.title: FEDS Note (Oct 16, 2026): U.S. stock-bond correlation 0.40 in 2000 to 2021, -0.09 post-2021; hedge "depends critically on the macroeconomic environment"
items.text: Li and Yoldas, "Government Bonds' Safe-Haven Property and Inflationary Pressures" (FEDS Notes, Oct 16, 2026), measure stock-bond correlation as the "correlation between stock returns and changes in 10-year government bond yields" (sample 1990-01-01 to 2026-07-31), so a positive value means bonds hedge stocks. United States: -0.26 pre-2000, 0.40 in 2000 to 2021, -0.09 post-2021 (euro area -0.28, 0.41, -0.02; UK -0.29, 0.31, -0.14). They write the "bond hedging property is not a fixed characteristic but depends critically on the macroeconomic environment"; with adverse supply shocks under above-target inflation, "In these cases, stock and bond prices can fall together." Post-2021 a one-unit U.S. inflation surprise moved 10-year yields 0.155 (t 4.93) versus 0.048 in 2000 to 2019 and cut stock returns 1.719 (t -3.04). "If inflationary pressures abate and the frequency of adverse supply shocks declines," the hedging property "is likely to improve."
items.source_title: Government Bonds' Safe-Haven Property and Inflationary Pressures (FEDS Notes)

items.text: Goldman Sachs Research (Hongcen Wei, Daan Struyven, Samantha Dart), May 20, 2026: US data center power demand of 31 GW in 2025, 41 GW in 2026 and 66 GW in 2027, which would "more than double the power used by US data centers within two years"; capacity reaches roughly 95 GW by end-2027 assuming 70% utilization. Realized capacity additions were 6.4 GW (2024) and 8.5 GW (2025); scheduled additions are 13.6 GW (2026) and 36.3 GW (2027), with 2.2 GW realized in Q1 2026 and 11.5 GW remaining for the year. Historically about 72% of data centers scheduled to activate within four quarters went online on time; Goldman forecasts about 60% on time over the next year and roughly 50% over the following two years. Data centers' share of US peak summer demand: 4.1% (2025), 5.3% (2026), 8.5% (2027).

items.title: Texas Aug 3, 2026: Abbott orders audit of data center queue; 17 loads (about 6.6 GW) cleared all gates but energization
items.text: Global Data Center Hub (industry newsletter) on the Texas large-load process: Governor Abbott's Aug 3, 2026 letter directed PUCT and ERCOT to audit data centers in the interconnection process and stated that "any project failing the review must be denied connection to the Texas grid"; the queue held more than 1,800 large-load requests totaling approximately 474 GW, roughly 90% data centers. The PUCT approved Batch Zero on Jun 18, 2026 for loads of 75 MW and above with default financial security of 50,000 dollars per MW where upgrade costs cannot be determined; 17 large loads totaling about 6.6 GW have cleared every gate except energization approval; ERCOT's all-time hourly peak was 91,089 MW on Jul 22, 2026. The audit covers about 250 to 300 projects, with ERCOT reports due Dec 10, 2026 for the PUCT's Dec 17 open meeting. Separately, PUCT docket 59220 (Jul 24, 2026) imposed a cumulative 525.5 MW uncompensated emergency curtailment obligation on two co-located data centers behind a 265.5 MW wind facility.
items.source_title: ERCOT data center interconnection pause: Docket 59220
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article dated Aug 26, 2026; Abbott letter Aug 3 and 'denied connection' quote verbatim; 1,800+ requests, 474 GW, 90%, Batch Zero Jun 18, 75 MW, $50,000/MW, 17 loads / 6.6 GW, 91,089 MW on Jul 22, 250-300 projects, Dec 10/17, docket 59220 Jul 24 with 525.5 MW and 265.5 MW all confirmed.

items.title: PJM 2026 load forecast: large load adjustments add 35.1 GW in 2026-2031, more than total demand growth of 34.6 GW
items.text: Modo Energy (Feb 27, 2026) on PJM's 2026 Long-Term Load Forecast: "summer peak demand will rise from 160 GW in 2025 to 253 GW by 2046, a 58% increase driven primarily by data centers"; "PJM's large load adjustments grow by 35.1 GW between 2026 and 2031, against total demand growth of 34.6 GW." Raw utility submissions of large load for 2030 totaled roughly 60 GW and "PJM accepted 34 GW, a 43% reduction before the forecast was published." Large load adjustments account for 78% of growth to 2046, and data centers in DOM, AEP, COMED and PL account for 74% of PJM's total annual demand growth from 2026 to 2046.
items.source_title: PJM load forecast: data centers drive 93 GW of growth through 2046
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Feb 27, 2026; 160 GW to 253 GW (58%) quote, 35.1 GW vs 34.6 GW quote, 60 GW submissions, '34 GW, a 43% reduction' quote, 78% and 74% shares all on page.

items.title: PJM 2028/2029 capacity auction (Jul 14, 2026): $325/MW-day at the cap, 6,831 MW short of the reliability requirement
items.text: PJM's 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction (results Jul 14, 2026) cleared at $325/MW-day (UCAP) across the entire PJM footprint, the FERC-approved cap, down 2.5% from the 2027/2028 cap of $333.44/MW-day. It procured 138,318 MW UCAP including demand response (149,182 MW UCAP with 10,864 MW of FRR), 6,831 MW below the reliability requirement, for a 14.7% reserve margin; cleared supply times clearing price equals $16.4 billion. New generation and uprates cleared only 525 MW UCAP; the forecast peak load is about 2,000 MW higher than for 2027/2028 as large data center loads keep entering the forecast. Cleared fuel mix: 46% natural gas (+5,639 MW UCAP), 20% nuclear, 18% coal (-2,941 MW), 5% demand response. PJM CEO David Mills: "These auction results show that demand for electricity continues to grow faster than electricity supply".
items.source_title: PJM Capacity Auction Procures 138,318 MW of Generation Resources as Work Continues To Address Growing Electricity Demand
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Jul 14, 2026; $325/MW-day cap RTO-wide, 2.5% below $333.44, 138,318 MW, 149,182 MW with 10,864 MW FRR, 6,831 MW short, 14.7%, $16.4B, 525 MW new/uprates, ~2,000 MW higher peak, fuel mix and +5,639/-2,941 MW, David Mills quote verbatim.

items.title: PJM 2028/2029 auction would have cleared at $554.72/MW-day without the collar; next auction closes Dec 15, 2026
items.text: Renewable Energy World / Factor This (Paul Gerke, Jul 16, 2026): without the price collar PJM's 2028/2029 auction would have cleared at $554.72 per MW-day for all zones, and PJM estimates the uncapped cost at "nearly $30 billion" versus the $16.4 billion actual. The 6,831 MW shortfall is against a 20% installed reserve margin target; PJM states "These most recent auctions were the first in PJM history in which the entire RTO fell short of the reliability requirement". The next auction, for the 2029/2030 delivery year, closes Dec 15 with the collar extended to it. A Synapse analysis cited puts annual capacity costs to customers at $14.7 billion, up from $2.2 billion in 2024.
items.source_title: PJM capacity auction easily hits price cap... Again
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Gerke, Jul 16, 2026; $554.72 uncapped, 'nearly $30 billion' vs $16.4B, 6,831 MW short of 20% IRM target, PJM 'first in PJM history' quote verbatim, Dec 15 close for 2029/2030 with collar extended, Synapse $2.2B (2024) to $14.7B all confirmed.

items.title: Minnesota PUC approves Xcel large load tariff May 15, 2026: 15-year minimum contract, 80% demand charge on early exit
items.text: Per Fresh Energy's regulatory update, the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission approved Xcel Energy's large load tariff on May 15, 2026: large facilities such as data centers take service under a minimum 15-year contract, face an "80% demand charge fee" if they exit early, and Xcel must create a separate large customer rate class for data centers so their costs can be assigned in future rate cases. Fresh Energy's Will Mulhern: "We are pleased the Commission has established a strong framework".
items.source_title: Regulatory Update: Commission approves Xcel Energy's large load tariff
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: May 15, 2026 approval, 15-year minimum, '80% demand charge fee', separate data center rate class and the Mulhern quote all on page.

items.title: GE Vernova Q2 2026: 116 GW of gas equipment backlog and slot reservations, target at least 125 GW by year-end 2026
items.text: GE Vernova's Q2 2026 release (Jul 22, 2026): Gas Power equipment backlog and slot reservation agreements reached 116 GW, up from 100 GW a quarter earlier. CEO Scott Strazik: "We now expect to have at least 125 GW of gas equipment under contract by year-end 2026" and "we remain on track to deliver 20 GW of annual gas turbine output in the third quarter of 2026", "with data center orders reaching over $5 billion year-to-date, more than double our 2025 total." Orders were $24.2B, up 88% organically; backlog $176 billion after growing $13.0B sequentially; revenue $11.1B, up 22%; adjusted EBITDA margin 11.3%, up 340 basis points organically; free cash flow $5.1B. CFO Ken Parks cited "healthy margins from favorable price and disciplined underwriting".
items.source_title: GE Vernova reports second quarter 2026 financial results and raises 2026 financial guidance

items.title: GE Vernova Q1 2026: about 10 GW of turbine slots left across 2029 and 2030, new orders priced 10 to 20 points higher per kW
items.text: Power Engineering (Kevin Clark, Apr 23, 2026) on GE Vernova's Q1 2026: 21 GW of new gas turbine agreements took total GW under contract from 83 to 100 GW (backlog 40 to 44 GW, slot reservations 43 to 56 GW). Entering Q1 about 10 GW of 2029 capacity was available; now about 10 GW remains across 2029 and 2030 combined, with heavy-duty gas turbine lead times of about three years. Per CEO Scott Strazik, H1 2026 new orders are priced 10 to 20 points higher per kW than Q4 2025 orders, and "the gas turbines are really not the gating item" for a 3-year project cycle. About 20% of orders are tied to data center load; data center-linked electrification orders reached $2.4 billion in Q1, exceeding all of 2025 combined. Wood Mackenzie projects gas turbine prices reaching $600/kW by end-2027, nearly triple 2019 levels.

items.title: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries large-frame gas turbine backlog 35 GW (up from 23 GW), new orders delivering 2028-2030
items.text: Utility Dive (Emma Penrod, Aug 13, 2026): Mitsubishi Heavy Industries' large-frame gas turbine backlog reached 35 GW, up from 23 GW a year earlier, after 10 large-frame orders in fiscal Q1 (4 for the US, 6 for Japan), with Energy Systems order intake up 56% year over year; orders booked this quarter are scheduled for delivery in 2028-2030. Fiscal 2025 sales were 35 large-frame turbines totaling 16 GW, and MHI plans to double production capacity relative to 2024 levels. items.title: Global gas turbine orders a record 38 GW in Q2 2026 (JP Morgan via Bloomberg); Wood Mackenzie sees $600/kW by 2027
items.text: Oilprice.com (Irina Slav, Aug 11, 2026), citing JP Morgan via Bloomberg: global gas turbine orders hit a record 38 GW in Q2 2026, up 29% from Q1 and 71% year over year, with Siemens Energy at 12.5 GW, GE at 11.3 GW and Mitsubishi Power at 5.3 GW; the United States accounted for half of new orders. Wood Mackenzie put end-2025 global orders at 110 GW against global manufacturing capacity of 60 to 70 GW, expects turbine prices to rise 195% by 2027 to $600 per kilowatt, and says "Turbine orders are expected to peak in 2026". BloombergNEF: combined-cycle plant lead times reached 5 years in 2025 from 3.5 years in 2023, with costs up 49%.

items.title: Reuters Jul 9, 2026: generator step-up transformer lead times passed 160 weeks by Q1 2026 (143 weeks in 2024)
items.text: Reuters (Jul 9, 2026, via AJOT): generator step-up transformer lead times surpassed 160 weeks by Q1 2026, compared with an average of 143 weeks in 2024, and high-voltage circuit breakers took 125 weeks in the second half of last year versus 77 weeks in 2023 (Wood Mackenzie data); some high-voltage transformers now take multiple years, up from around one year in 2020 and 2021, and transformer costs could rise by around 4% to up to 10% over the next year depending on type. Roseville Electric Utility (California) has moved from buying about a year out to a three-year timeline and is buying for projects five years ahead. Wood Mackenzie's Ben Boucher: "Equipment availability is becoming the biggest concern for developers as they value time to market so highly".
items.source_title: US power companies scramble to secure equipment as surging data center demand strains supplies
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Reuters via AJOT, Jul 9, 2026; 160 weeks by Q1 2026 vs 143 in 2024, 125 vs 77 weeks breakers, multi-year vs ~1 year in 2020-21, 4% to 10% cost rise, Roseville 1 to 3 years and 5 years ahead, Boucher quote verbatim.

items.title: Cushman & Wakefield 2026 cost guide: US and Canada greenfield data center cost $17.6M per MW, up 21% since Q4 2024
items.text: Cushman & Wakefield's 2026 Data Center Development Cost Guide (press release Sep 3, 2026): the all-in greenfield development cost for the United States and Canada averages $17.6M per MW, excluding chips and GPUs, and costs rose an average of 21% per MW since the previous edition published in Q4 2024, driven by supply chain constraints, rising skilled labor wages, land fundamentals and escalating component costs; Texas markets "continue to rank among the lowest-cost development environments". items.title: Google-Constellation Oct 6, 2026: 20-year PPA for 890 MW of nuclear uprates plus 15-year 2,700 MW supply deal
items.text: BIC Magazine (Oct 6, 2026): Google and Constellation announced a 20-year power purchase agreement that adds 890 MW of new nuclear capacity to the PJM grid through uprates at 11 Constellation units across six sites in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, a separate 15-year energy supply agreement covering 2,700 MW of existing generation, and an expanded five-year technology alliance with Google Cloud and Gemini Enterprise. Constellation will invest more than $4.3 billion; the first uprate is expected online by 2028. Google's Amanda Peterson Corio: "Our agreement with Constellation to fund nuclear reactor uprates will strengthen the PJM grid".

items.title: CBRE H1 2026: 7,481 MW under construction in eight primary markets, over 80% preleased, Northern Virginia vacancy 0.2%
items.text: CBRE press release (Sep 8, 2026), North America Data Center Trends H1 2026: 7,481 MW under construction across the eight primary markets, up 24.8% and above the prior 2024 high; more than 80% of capacity under construction is preleased (74.3% a year earlier) and less than 1,500 MW remains available for preleasing, roughly six months of supply at the current pace; primary-market vacancy 1.4%; net absorption 1,456 MW, up nearly 12%. Northern Virginia: inventory 4,496.5 MW, vacancy 0.2% (0.7% a year earlier), 10.8 MW available, 2,420.2 MW under construction. Asking rents rose for every deployment size, the largest increase 8.3% for 3 MW to 10 MW users. CBRE's Stu Dyer: "Power is the deciding factor in Northern Virginia right now".

items.title: SynMax via Power Engineering Oct 5, 2026: nearly 40% of US data center projects due in 2026 at risk of slipping over three months
items.text: Power Engineering (Bethany Bashioum, Oct 5, 2026), citing geospatial analytics firm SynMax: "Nearly 40% of U.S. data center projects scheduled for completion this year" could miss their targets by more than three months, with labor shortages, equipment constraints, permitting and power access cited. Named cases: Project Jupiter (New Mexico), whose supporting gas pipeline is "running roughly six months behind schedule", pushing completion to Feb 2027; Project Lighthouse (Wisconsin), where Aterio estimates partial power in Dec 2027 versus Oracle's second-half 2027 target and full 1.3 GW by Oct 2028 after regulators required ATC to restart its transmission application; Stargate (Texas), whose ramp "has taken longer than some early estimates suggested"; and Microsoft's Licking County, Ohio site slowed by weather. Grid connections in major markets can take three to four years.

items.title: Mar 2026: Oracle and OpenAI scrap 600 MW Abilene expansion; committed build about 1.2 GW
items.text: Tom's Hardware (Luke James, Mar 10, 2026): Oracle and OpenAI scrapped a planned 600 MW expansion lease at the Abilene, Texas Stargate campus (first reported by Bloomberg on Mar 6, followed by Reuters) that would have pushed the site toward 2 GW; the committed build is roughly 1.2 GW on 1,000 acres with eight buildings, two running workloads and the remaining six due by mid-2026. Reasons reported included failed financing negotiations and a multi-day winter outage that took buildings offline by disrupting liquid cooling; The Information reported power at the expansion site would not be ready for roughly a year. Oracle called the coverage "false and incorrect" and said the Abilene site "remains on schedule"; the broader 4.5 GW Oracle-OpenAI agreement (Jul 2025) remained on track.

items.title: xAI Colossus 2 runs about 1,300 MW of behind-the-meter gas with no utility power (Cleanview, mid-May 2026)
items.text: Cleanview's behind-the-meter data center report (timeline through May 2026): xAI's Colossus 2 (Whitehaven, Memphis, Tennessee) runs on about 1,300 MW of gas generation at the Southaven, Mississippi power plant site, all behind the meter, with no utility power and no large natural gas pipeline. Satellite imagery in mid-May 2026 showed 59 turbines (MDEQ subsequently confirmed 46 temporary-mobile units); MDEQ approved air permits in Mar 2026 for 41 permanent generators (about 1.2 GW), none yet installed and under appeal by SELC since Apr 2026; xAI ordered 5 Doosan DGT6-300H S2 H-class turbines (1,900 MW). Colossus 1 has about 198 MW on-site gas plus 300 MW of grid supply, about 500 MW total. xAI said its data centers "cannot currently function" without the turbines; utilities had given xAI timelines of years, and xAI built its first data center in 4 months.

items.text: Reuters (Summer Zhen and Anirban Sen, Oct 23, 2026) reports that three major strategies tracked by Goldman Sachs, fundamental equity long-short, systematic and multi-strategy, each lost more than 1% on Oct 22, 2026, the first such day since the COVID pandemic. Goldman's prime brokerage team wrote: "If last Thursday felt bad, today has been worse." Losses were concentrated in China and technology holdings plus a squeeze in crowded shorts, and "losses in crowded AI-linked trades forced investors to cut exposure and rein in risk." The Nasdaq's 2.6% fall was its largest since June 5.
items.source_title: Hedge fund returns worsen this week as tech selloff deepens

items.title: BofA October 2026 FMS: short Treasuries the second most crowded trade at 27%
items.text: Mace News' summary of the BofA Global Fund Manager Survey released Tuesday Oct 13, 2026 (fieldwork Oct 2 to Oct 8, 185 panelists with $512bn AUM): cash 3.9% of AUM, up from an "uber-low" 3.5% in August; global equities net 44% overweight (49% in September); bonds net 37% underweight (48% in September); US equities net 11% overweight (25% in September). Most crowded trades: long global semiconductors 45% (53% in September, 82% July record), short Treasuries 27% (18% in September), long Magnificent 7 16% (7%). Top tail risks: disorderly rise in bond yields 31%, AI bubble 23%, second wave of inflation 20%. Asked what 10-year yield would prompt a shift from stocks to bonds, 37% said 6.0% and 19% said yields are already there.
items.source_title: BofA Global Research Fund Manager Survey: Lower Growth and Lower Inflation Expectations Lead to Tweaking of Asset Allocations in October
items.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Fieldwork Oct 2 to 8, 185 panelists / $512bn, cash 3.9% vs 'uber-low' 3.5% in August, equities net 44% (49%), bonds net 37% underweight (48%), US equities net 11% (25%), crowded trades 45%/27%/16% with priors, tail risks 31/23/20, and 37% / 19% on the yield question all on the page; the page says only 'released Tuesday', and Oct 13, 2026 is confirmed by an investinglive report dated 13 Oct 2026.
